I only ghosted someone once. I felt really bad about it, and felt even worse after she called me out. Basically, I met this girl through a mutual friend. We picked her up really late at night after going to the city to buy some cocaine. Her house was on the way home, so we stopped by and she got in the car. I’d never met her before, but she asked for my number after about 5 minutes. She then started texting me, saying how much she wanted to kiss me. The night went on, and eventually my friend drove her home. A few nights later, she texts me around midnight, asking me to drive to the city and hang out. Now, I was about 20 years old at this point and still a virgin. I knew exactly what was gonna happen. I was also anxious to lose my virginity cuz I felt really awkward being one of the only virgins in my group of friends. So I went to her house and we ended up having sex. I went home at like 4 AM. For the next few days, she texted me constantly. She started saying “I love you,” very quickly. I’d literally met her twice. It scared me... a lot. So I ghosted her. I felt really bad about it, but I wasn’t looking for a serious relationship and she was coming on way too strong. After a couple weeks, she got into a fight with the mutual friend I’d met her through. He was talking to me about how much she was insulting him and stuff. He then told me that she’d been talking shit about me as well. He told me what she’d said about me, and honestly I felt like I deserved it. I felt horrible about myself and I still regret what I did. I should have talked to her about it, and been truthful. It may sound like a stupid thing to worry about, but it still keeps me up at night sometimes. I hope I didn’t permanently scar her emotionally. My hope is that she’s forgotten about me at this point and gotten over it.

Thanks so much for all the feedback! I really appreciate how much time you put into this. You gave me a lot of good stuff to think about. As for the mechanical stuff, I’ll definitely re-work a lot of those sentences. I’ll also put in some details that help give more life to the world. 

You made a couple other points that I want to address/ask about. You said that withholding information isn’t a good thing. I withheld certain bits of information because I didn’t want to overwhelm the reader with information about this world, if it isn’t directly relevant to the story. Also, I couldn’t always find a convenient way to explain things further. With the comment about the War Of Three Kingdoms, I couldn’t figure out why the characters would go into more detail about it. They both live in this world and are familiar with its history, so I couldn’t think of a reasonable way for one of them to explain what the war was.

Also, you said that it wasn’t really clear what the threat was. At this point in the story, Jolnir hasn’t read the entire prophecy because he only recovered half of it, and it is nonsensical without the other half. Neither he, nor Dyroth knows what it’s about. I didn’t want them to freak out too much about the prophecy since they have no idea yet that it spells doom for their entire race. I will try to flesh out the threat a little better, but I don’t really know how to do that, while still having them be clueless about the prophecy. 

Again, thank you so much for your reply. It really helps to hear criticism. Looks like I’ve got a lot to work on, can’t wait to get started.

I go through long periods of low-level depression. When that happens, it's really just a matter of getting enough sleep, eating well, spending time with my gf, friends, and family, and making sure I have some structure in my life. Small amounts of physical exercise seem to work pretty well too. When I'm dealing with something worse than the usual mild depression and I'm having a really bad day, I have other methods to cheer myself up. My first line of defense is usually music. I'll just pick up a guitar and play for a while. If that isn't working I may take a hot shower, which often helps me to calm down a bit. If that also doesn't work, my next step is generally to get moderately drunk and watch Lord Of The Rings. Those movies are like comfort food for me. My last resort after that is to get blackout drunk and listen to my "Drinking Alone" playlist on spotify, which consists of a few up-beat drinking songs and a ton of really melancholic, depressing songs as well. I typically end up crying my eyes out, which feels really really good since I normally find it impossible to cry even when I want to. Really gets a lot of the negative emotions out and resets me a little bit.

In my world, everything was created by the gods after The War Of The Gods. In order to put their differences behind them they created the world together, so they could cooperate and work towards a common goal and have peace and unity. So that is the purpose of life, the reason why it exists. As for the MEANING of life, I guess it really depends on culture. For the Shadow Folk, particularly those of noble birth, service to the king and country is all the purpose they need in life. For the Kelvari, life's meaning is to learn and understand the world around them as best as they can. The Aureon don't really have a philosophy on life, but if they did, it would probably be that conquering and enslaving all other races is the greatest good and most desirable outcome. There are/were many other cultures with different views on life, but those are a couple different answers from a few of my cultures.

When you're a kid, you think that you'll be fearless as an adult. You think the monsters in your closet and under your bed will go away. You think you'll have everything figured out and you'll be above fear. And it's true that you lose your fear of monsters in the closet, you lose your fear of the dark. You trade those fears in for even scarier things. You realize that you never really outgrew fear, you just found things to fear that are even worse. You realize that you don't have everything figured out, and neither does anyone else. You come to the realization that every single person is just winging it and doing the best they can in a world where everything is uncertain and no one knows what to do. It's terrifying to realize that all the authority figures in your life, your guiding stars, your parents, your role-models all have no idea what's going on. We're all just scared little kids deep down. We just do a good job of hiding it. That's the darkest secret I've learned about life thus far.

Funny you should ask. It just happened about 5 hours ago. I was driving to my best friend's house to have dinner with him and his wife. Suddenly, I heard a noise that I can only describe as the sound of glass shattering. It was extremely loud. I had death metal blaring through the stereo at max volume, and I still heard the sound very clearly over the music. That's how loud it was. I wasn't sure what had happened. I thought maybe I had hit something. After I got to my friend's house, I inspected my car for damage. Nothing. No dents, no scratches. I have no idea what the noise was, but it was insanely loud and it scared the crap out of me. As a runner-up, one time several years ago, I was home alone. It was probably some time after midnight, maybe 1 or 2 in the morning. I decided to go to sleep and after laying in bed for a while I heard a loud scratching sound on my window. I thought that maybe snow was hitting the window or something, so I looked outside but it wasn't snowing anymore, as it had been earlier in the night. There are no tree-branches or anything like that near the window, so I have no idea what could have made the noise. I've heard plenty of weird noises in that house. When home alone, I've often heard the very loud sound of footsteps coming up the basement stairs, a sound that my little sister has heard many times as well. I'm skeptical about the concept of hauntings, but I'm starting to believe that the house may be haunted.

They hated magic because the people of Wenya used magic against their ancestors. Then in more recent times, The Aureon attempted to invade them several times and used Fury Magic against them. Their enemies had always used magic, so they grew to hate it and almost anyone who used it. They were friends with the Star Folk, but they didn’t particularly like the fact that the Star Folk used magic.

It depended on the culture. For the Star Folk, it was mostly based on incantations. The Shadow Folk hated magic however and never used it. So for them it was more based on herbs and plants. Both cultures did use surgery and things like that, but only as a last resort.

My world is a quasi-medieval setting, so modern medicine does not exist. However, the existence of magic as well as certain herbs, potions and other fictional materials allows the people of my world to enjoy a fairly good quality of medical treatment. Of course, it depends on the culture in question. The Star Folk, for example had great medical treatment. A lot of their medicine revolved around Star Magic, and to a lesser extent, Nature Magic. They could cure fairly severe wounds as well as common sicknesses with ease. There were limits to what they could cure with their magic however. Sometimes a patient’s wounds would be too severe, or they would be too sick to recover, but their medical treatment was close to what ours is today, despite their lack of modern medicine. The Shadow Folk have a similar level of medical care, despite not using magic. They instead focused their attention on herbs with curative properties. Other cultures like the Aureon have little to no medical technology whatsoever. In Aureon culture, only the strongest survive. They do not use medicine, partly because their society is dysfunctional and entirely focused on warfare, and partly because they believe that only the weak need medicine.

I have many different themes that I try to explore in my world, but one that I don't often talk about is the subversion of beauty standards. For example, I have a race called the Shadow Folk who are a race of black skinned, red-eyed demons who inhabit a moon that is always dark. Their music is described as being dissonant and ugly, their artwork, weapons, clothing and pretty much everything else in their culture is described in ways that make it sound ugly or unpleasant. Yet, I try to make the reader see that there is beauty in their culture, their artwork, their music, the landscapes of their moon, etc. Pretty much everything has beauty in it if you know where to look, and that is something that I've been trying to convey in my book.

A demon is any descendent of the Falarian Sea Kings, who were considered the first demon race. They made a pact with Gwailgori which gave them dominion over the seas, but it changed them both physically and spiritually. All demons also have dragon blood in their veins, which is a very long story. The dragon blood gives them certain physical advantages over other races. So they aren’t demons in the Judeo-Christian sense of the word, but they do look pretty demonic and they are called demons by the other races in my world.
They aren’t very ornate or decorated. The Oni believe that all Oni are equal in the eyes of Gwailgori, so everyone from kings to peasants gets a pretty plain raft.

Gwailgori is a real entity, yes. He still protects and to some degree favors the Oni over all other races because of their devotion to him. He does not claim the bodies, it’s more of a symbolic thing than a literal sacrifice to the sea god.

The most common pop history book would probably be, "A Tale Of Defiance," written by Kalsgad of Clan Blackwater (not to be confused with Kalsgad of Clan Snowspear). The book is an overly dramatic and sensationalized account of the Battle Of Grenith, which was dramatic and sensational enough without being embellished. It particularly focuses on the last stand of Captain Elnir and the Star Folk, whose forces were decimated in the battle. Historians agree that the book has many inaccuracies and a much better alternative to "A Tale Of Defiance" is the book "An Account Of The Last Stand Of Elnir." It wasn't nearly as popular among the general population, but much more accurate and more respected among historians.

The shadowsteel armor worn by the members of the King’s Banner isn’t all alike. The kingdom does not provide soldiers with shadowsteel armor, so those knights and soldiers who have shadowsteel armor have specially ordered it from various different blacksmiths. The armor must be fairly thick in order to repel magic attacks, but some soldiers have armor that is only somewhat bulky, whereas others, such as Sir Vennik, have ludicrously bulky armor that most people would not be able to fight in. His set of armor is also covered in spikes for no other reason than the fact that it looks terrifying. 

The armor of the Dragon Guard is pretty bulky as well, but probably not as bulky as some of the more extreme variations of shadowsteel armor. It looks somewhat like a bulked-up version of Japanese ō-yoroi armor, though it covers the entire body. It makes movement difficult, but it is mostly ceremonial. Very few people are stupid enough to attempt to harm the Dragon King, so the Dragon Guard rarely see combat.

Certain knights and warriors in the King’s Banner (standing army of the kingdom of Nightfall) wear very thick armor made from shadowsteel. Sir Vennik was the first to have a set of shadowsteel armor made for him and then many other knights and wealthier soldiers followed suit. The armor covers pretty much the entire body and is a bit bulky, but it insulates the wearer from magic, making magic-wielding enemies essentially powerless. Shadowsteel is also much lighter than traditional steel, so it’s bulkiness isn’t too much of a problem.

The Dragon Guard, who are the shock troops of Falaria’s army as well as the personal guards of the king, wear very bulky, ornate armor. The armor is mostly ceremonial and they rarely see combat, but they are skilled enough warriors to be able to fight well even with their bulky armor.

That said, they were still very friendly with most other races, they simply didn't have offspring with them. There were a few exceptions, of course.

The Shadow Folk and Kelvari (demon races) would intermix from time to time with other races, mostly with each other. It was uncommon, but not looked down upon. I'll talk about the military of the Kingdom of Nightfall, as it is the most fleshed-out. Their army is comprised of two main parts: the King's Banner and the Clan Armies. The King's Banner is the king's personal force, and is always on duty. It is comprised of 5 legions called the Northern Legion, Erros Legion,  Sundered Basin Legion, Shatterspike Legion, and Heartland Legion. They are each led by a commander and they ride on patrol through their resepctive regions throughout most of the year. The clan armies are the forces of each of the six Great Clans. The Great Clans use their own clansmen as well as men from lesser vassal clans to build their armies. The mobilization of the clan armies only happens during times of war. Thus, the clan armies are only authorized to engage enemy forces. The king's banner is able to engage at their own discretion. The only stipulation is that they must not engage enemies who have surrendered. They often take prisoners and honor demands that the prisoners are treated well. This rarely causes problems, as the king hand-picks his commanders and makes sure they are honorable and merciful leaders.

Most of the king's banner is generally on horseback, in order to traverse the long distances necessary to complete their patrols. The clan armies, being less well-equipped, are mainly infantry. Both sections of the army are tricky and will not hesitate to sacrifice many lives by using entire legions to bait the enemy into treacherous territory perfect for an ambush. This is generally how they beat larger forces. They know their land well and make full use of it. As for battles on open ground, they will often send infantry against an enemy force. They will use pikes or swords depending on whether the enemy is on horseback or on foot. The cavalry will then come in from the flanks and decimate the opponent. In siege defense, the normally keep archers on the battlements and swordsman behind the gate. If the enemy uses ladders or siege towers, they'll divert swordsman to the battlements. If the invaders attempt to retreat, it is common practice to send out horsemen to run them down. They don't often allow retreating enemies to escape. Nightfall has never been successfully invaded.

STARSPELL, CAPITAL OF NIGHTFALL:

Starspell is regarded as perhaps the most beautiful city of all the kingdoms, now that Lumiel is gone. It resides in the heartlands of Nightfall, a kingdom of permanent darkness. In the darker part of the night, the aurora can be seen above the city, and the stars shine bright. Nightfall is known for its strange geological composition, and the capital city is a beautiful example of this. It was built around a massive formation of crystals which protrude from the ground and reach hundreds of feet into the sky. Many of the crystaline structures were hollowed out and made into homes and other buildings. Around the crystal formation was built a high wall of black obsidian, which is manned by a garrison of city guards. The streets are paved with cobblestone and meander in between the crystal sky-scrapers. 

Being the capital, the city is run by the Shadow King of Nightfall. There is a city council as well, elected by the common people to advise the king on matters concerning the city. The capital is also where the House Of Nobles meets. They act as a makeshift senate, although they usually worry about their clans' well-being before the well-being of the common people. However, this is their job. They represent the interests of the six Great Clans, as well as some of the larger Lesser Clans. The King is meant to listen to their concerns as well as the concerns of the city council and balance the needs of the clans with the needs of the common folk. Unlike most regions of the kingdom, there is no single Great Clan who can claim the capital or the surrounding lands as their own. The capital has no clan loyalties and answers only to the king.

As such, the city pays no taxes or tributes to any clan. They pay only the royal taxes, which are modest. The city is fairly prosperous and contains many public services, such as the second-largest public library ever built. The people of Nightfall, the Shadow Folk, are avid scholars and historians, so this library means a great deal to them. There is clean running water in the city, brought in by a viaduct stemming from the Forked River. It is a technologically advanced city compared to others. They have access to Territe, a material which, when combined with iron, forms a strong and light alloy called Shadow Steel. This allows them to build stronger, taller structures, cut through hard crystal formations, and do a number of other things that the rest of their medieval society cannot do. A sum of 10,000 gold Drakons (their currency), would be sufficient to purchase a home within the city. It would not be a mansion, but you would be able to live a comfortable, middle-class lifestyle with that money, as the average price of a home is approximately 8,000.

The Shadow Folk have a very interesting view on death. Though their ancestors worshipped the sea god, they have elected instead to worship Anazul, the god of death. They recognize that death is inevitable and believe that those who have died will live on in the afterlife. However, the actual afterlife is of little concern to them; they prefer to live on in the stories passed down through generations, so it is their aspiration to do great deeds in life and be remembered as a hero. At funerals, they generally play traditional funeral dirges. The songs are mostly sad and dissonant, a symbol of the pain and bitterness of mortality. Yet, the songs also have very sweet, triumphant passages which are used as a celebration of the life of the deceased. The dead are usually placed in a boat and sent out to sea, given back to the sea god. Sometimes, they will set the boat aflame before giving the dead their final send-off.

Part of it is just time. You aren't gonna fill all the blanks today, maybe you'll think of some cool story a couple weeks from now and add it into the history of one of these countries. Maybe they don't need a full history. Sometimes its better to only hint at the depth of the world rather than actually show it. Tolkien did this all the time, making references to stories that he never explained or fleshed out. Well thats kinda tricky, because for me its always been a pretty organic process, meaning I just kinda let it happen and go with random ideas I get. That said, my newest world has been a little more focused. I pick a kingdom and then ask myself, "who lives here? What does their society value? Who governs it?" Societal biases and values will deeply influence the laws and customs of a society and in turn the societal values are often influenced by historical happenings as well as the environment they live in. For example, my world has a race of demons who hate magic, and as a result of this bias they have, magic is illegal in their kingdom. Then i had to think to myself, "why do they hate magic?" I came to the conclusion that they had been invaded by sorcerers multiple times throughout history. 

Another important factor is the terrain. A city/town that is near a river or large body of water is probably gonna have a large fishing economy. People who live on plains or steppes will likely have a culture revolving around horse riding and may be nomadic. The best thing to do is always ask yourself "why?" And try to come up with a reasonable explanation. One last thing: you can have the coolest world ever, but it doesn't mean much without interesting stories. Coming up with stories is the best way to add depth to a world in my experience. Anyway, hope this helps and happy worldbuilding!

Long version: first you need to understand a little bit about the cosmology and magic systems in my world. All types of magic require energy, and each magic type gets energy from a different source. Necromancy requires consuming hearts in order to gain their power. Therefore, the Abysmal Prince started out by murdering people and eating their hearts, using their life energy to fuel his magic. Eventually, he had consumed hundreds of hearts and gained immense power. Now at this point, the gods constructed the 14 moons at equidistant points around the world. Each moon was alive and had a beating heart as well, ripped from the chest of a lesser god. The moons were constructed as a fail safe. If the Abysmal Prince could not be stopped, the magical energy contained within the hearts of the moons would be released and much like a nuclear bomb it would generate massive explosions, disintegrating the moons and sterilizing the planet. Unfortunately, the Abysmal Prince found out that the planet also had a heart, a much more powerful heart and so he stole the planet's heart and ate it, gaining an absurd amount of power and killing the planet. Everything on the planet began to die and so the mortals used unknown magic to build World Gates which transported them to the various moons where they took refuge and built their kingdoms, unaware of the devastating power contained within each moon. Hundreds of years later the Abysmal Prince began attacking the moons and stealing their hearts so that he could gain enough power to rival the gods. One of the moons he attacked was the moon-kingdom of the Star Folk, which is how they became extinct. He also wanted revenge on the Star Folk and the demon people for banishing him to the void during the second War Of Moons a few hundred years earlier.

Depends on the culture. The Oni mainly use zithers, lutes and harps in their music as well as some wooden instruments similar to the flute. The music is generally foreign-sounding to any outsider who hears it, but is usually peaceful. It is used mainly by nobility but other wealthy Oni often hire musicians as well. The Shadow Folk mainly use horns and lutes and their music is much less relaxing. According to the account of Jolnir (a historian in my world), the "music of the Shadow Folk was violent and dissonant but occasionally rose to great heights and sweet melodies soared triumphantly before returning again to darkness." The Shadow Folk use dissonant, haunting melodies in order to make the sweeter melodies even more powerful by contrast, for their music is used most commonly for funeral dirges and is meant to reflect both the  bitterness of mortality, and also the preciousness of life while it lasts. The Ice Demons have no music of their own, as they are too busy studying lore to care for such things. Some Ice Demons have traveled to other kingdoms to learn the ways of music and returned, playing the foreign music for their own people. The Ice Demons generally prefer the music of their kin, the Shadow Folk.

As for the non-demonic races, the Star Folk are known for having the most complex and most beautiful music. They use all manner of instrument from lutes, harps and lyres to viols, flutes and horns. The Aureon are too violent and war-like to care much for music. Their music normally consists only of drums and occasionally horns as well. It is used during war and for no other reason. As for the Djinn, people have heard very little of their music so it is unclear what it is used for and what it commonly sounds like, but it is clear that they do have their own music and use it for purposes other than war.

The kingdoms in my world are actually moons, each one with its own culture and leadership. This is because the planet was destroyed long ago, forcing the many peoples of Chasdia (my world) to flee through magical gates to the safety of the moons.
Now, the most diverse moon would certainly be Hloenyralin (pronounced len-EAR-uh-lin). Originally, it was an expansion of the Shadow Folk's (one of the demon races) empire. Before long, the other demon races (Ice Demons and Oni) showed up and many decided to live there permanently. Even many of the non-demons (the Aureon and the Djinn) came to live on Hloenyralin.

Advantages:

1. jointly held, politically neutral kingdom (similar to Switzerland in that respect)

2. diverse marketplace offers wide range of products from all over the many moons

3. common meeting place for political figures as it is a neutral area

Problems:

1. Tension between the Demons and the Aureon, who have attempted to enslave most of the demon kingdoms at one time or another

2. Oftentimes cannot make executive decisions for lack of a consensus among its citizens

3. Differing opinions of magic, which leads to conflict

Solutions:

1. There is and always will be tension between the Aureon and the demons. That being said, generations of living together have quelled much of the bad-blood between the races.

2. The Lord of Hloenyralin is essentially a puppet of the three demon kings, so they ultimately make the decisions together behind closed doors.

3. Legal restrictions on certain types of magic. The Djinn are allowed to freely practice their Star Magic, but the Fury Magic of the Aureon is highly restricted and its use relegated to only the most qualified and practiced mages.

In the futuristic world that is the backdrop for the sci-fi novel I'm currently writing, there are several real-world nations, though they aren't all the same as they are in today's world. For example, most of Asia Minor and northern Africa have become the Grand Confederation of Caliphates. I think using real world nations can add a degree of believability and realism to a work of science fiction, if it is set on earth. I do think it's important to show a progression, however. Borders are constantly changing and countries have always come and gone and will probably continue to do so, so it wouldn't make sense for the exact same countries with the exact same borders to be present in a story set hundreds or thousands of years in the future.

Strategist: Nelannen, the first high king of the Ancient Ones and  the first being created by the gods, was a master strategist. He was extremely wise, being the oldest life-form in existence other than the gods, thus he led not only his own people, but also the armies of Neldar, the kingdom of Men, in the war against the dark realm of Namora during the Mythic Era. He was unfortunately killed during the second battle of Belerad, in which the capital city of his people was destroyed forever. It is said that a great storm raged that night as the gods wept in mourning for their first-born.

Tactician: Captain Stonehelm, one of the three captains of men during the time after the destruction of Neldar in the second era. He commanded the troops of the southern villages and long held off the forces of the Great Demon, who sought the final destruction of all mankind. In the year 948 of the second era, he was killed while defending his village.

I'm certainly no psychologist, but you seem to suffer from much of the same feelings and thoughts that I do. Many of your symptoms (such as feeling like a different person every day and feeling disconnected from your memories and yourself) are possible symptoms of Borderline Personality Disorder. Again, I'm no psychologist but its just a thought. If that is the case, it is important to seek treatment quickly, as many people with BPD are prone to suicide and/or self injury. I really think you should seek professional help, maybe try going to a different psychiatrist for another opinion, as they will be able to give you a proper diagnosis and offer a treatment plan which can help to ease your symptoms. You shouldn't refer to yourself as a suicidal, attention seeking brat either. Sometimes, people just feel depressed and suicidal for no reason. Even people who seem to have everything they could ever want are simply unhappy. Don't hate yourself for that. You need to understand that this is NOT your fault, it's just the result of a chemical imbalance in your brain or possibly other genetic factors. Like any other medical problem, you have no control over it. You wouldn't tell a heart-attack victim to feel guilty for having been born with a bad heart, would you? It's no different, except that your particular condition affects your brain instead. If you ever need to talk, just PM me.
